resources.string: In short
Typical
How the controller drives the motor. FOC runs it smoothly and quietly with sine-shaped currents; BLDC switches in six steps and is only worth it for old setups that were tuned for it.
FOC.
The most current the motor gets while accelerating, which sets the strongest pull. This is motor (phase) current; the battery sees less at low speed.
At or under the motor\'s rating and well under the controller\'s. Electric skateboards often run 50 to 70 A per motor, hub-motor bikes 30 to 50 A.
The most current the motor gets while braking, as a negative number. Sets how hard the brake can grab.
The same size as the acceleration limit or a little smaller, negative.
The most current taken from the battery. Protects the pack and its BMS; it limits top-end power more than launch torque.
The battery\'s continuous discharge rating, divided among the controllers that share it.
The most current pushed back into the battery while braking, as a negative number. A full battery or a weak one tolerates little.
Within the battery\'s charge rating, often -5 to -15 A per controller.
A safety trip: if any phase current spikes above this, the controller cuts the motor and logs an over-current fault. It is a last line of defence, not a limit the motor runs at.
About 1.3 to 1.5 times the motor current limit, and below the controller\'s hardware limit. Firmware 6.05 and newer warns when it is closer than 1.3 times.
Battery voltage where the controller starts to reduce power, so an emptying pack isn\'t pulled into deep discharge.
About 3.3 to 3.4 V per cell for lithium-ion, times the cell count.
Battery voltage where power reaches zero. Between start and end the power ramps down.
About 3.0 to 3.1 V per cell for lithium-ion, times the cell count.
Below this input voltage the controller stops driving the motor and reports an under-voltage fault.
Under the battery cutoff end, so cutoff ramps power down before this trips.
Above this input voltage the controller stops and reports an over-voltage fault, for example when braking into a full battery.
A little above the fully charged pack voltage, and below what the controller is rated for.
Highest motor speed forward, in electrical RPM: mechanical RPM times the number of pole pairs.
The controller\'s rated maximum, often 60 000 to 100 000 ERPM. Lower it to cap top speed.
Highest motor speed in reverse, as a negative number.
The negative of the forward limit, or much smaller if reverse should be slow.
Controller temperature where it starts reducing current to cool down.
Controller temperature where current reaches zero.
Motor temperature where current starts to drop. Only works with a temperature sensor in the motor and the matching sensor type set.
80 to 90 °C for common hobby motors; higher only for windings rated for it.
Motor temperature where current reaches zero.
100 to 110 °C for common hobby motors.
The highest share of the battery voltage the controller applies. Sets top speed together with battery voltage and the motor\'s speed constant.
Power limit while accelerating, on top of the current limits.
Leave it high unless a legal power cap applies.
Power limit while braking, negative.
Leave it at a large negative number unless the battery needs gentler regen.
Winding resistance, measured by motor detection.
Whatever detection measured; edit by hand only to copy a known-good value.
Winding inductance, measured by motor detection.
Whatever detection measured.
How strongly the magnets link the windings; it sets how voltage relates to speed. Measured by detection.
Whatever detection measured.
How hard the current controller reacts to an error. Computed from the motor\'s resistance and inductance during detection.
The computed value. Too high whines or vibrates; too low gives sluggish torque.
How fast the current controller removes a steady error. Computed during detection.
The computed value.
Where the controller gets the rotor position: from the motor\'s back-EMF (sensorless), hall sensors, an encoder, or high-frequency injection at standstill.
Hall sensors when the motor has them and starts from a standstill under load; sensorless otherwise.
How often the controller switches its outputs. Higher is quieter and smoother on low-inductance motors but heats the controller more.
25 to 30 kHz.
How quickly the sensorless position estimate follows the motor. Computed from the flux linkage during detection.
The computed value.
Below this speed sensorless mode can\'t see the rotor and spins the field blindly to get going.
Detection\'s value; lower makes starts gentler but less reliable.
Speed where hall or encoder sensing hands over to sensorless.
Detection\'s value, often 2 000 to 4 000 ERPM.
Swaps forward and reverse without swapping motor wires.
Whatever makes forward go forward; the Direction tool sets it by spinning the motor.
Cells in series in the battery. Used for the battery cutoff suggestions and for percentage estimates.
The pack\'s S count, for example 10 for a 10S pack.
Battery capacity, for range and percentage estimates.
The pack\'s rated amp-hours.
Wheel diameter, used to turn motor speed into vehicle speed and distance.
Measured across the tyre, not the rim.
Magnet poles in the motor (not pole pairs). Turns electrical RPM into mechanical RPM.
14 for most outrunners, often 46 or more for hub motors.
Motor turns per wheel turn.
1 for hub and direct drive; the pulley or gear ratio otherwise.
This controller\'s address on the CAN bus. Every device on the bus needs its own.
0 for the first, 1 for the second, and so on.
Which input drives the motor: PPM (receiver), ADC (throttle and brake levers), UART (remote or module on the UART port), and so on.
What the throttle is wired to. Pick an app with UART if a Bluetooth or WiFi module sits on the UART port.
If no input arrives for this long, the controller releases the motor. Protects against a lost remote or a cut wire.
Brake current applied after a timeout instead of coasting.
0 A on vehicles where a sudden brake could throw the rider; a few amps on robots.
Bit rate of the CAN bus. Every device on the bus must match; the CAN bus tool changes it for all of them at once.
500 kbit/s.
What the receiver\'s stick controls: current, duty, speed, with or without reverse or brake.
Current, no reverse with brake, for vehicles.
How far the stick must move before the controller switches between driving and braking.
How long the command takes to climb from zero to full. Softens jerky throttle input.
0.3 to 0.5 s for vehicles.
How long the command takes to fall from full to zero.
0.1 to 0.3 s; shorter than the climb so letting go responds quickly.
How the throttle (and brake) voltages map to the motor.
Current, no reverse with brake ADC2, for a throttle and a brake lever.
Throttle voltage at rest. The ADC mapping tool reads it from the throttle.
Hall throttles rest near 0.8 to 0.9 V.
Throttle voltage at full.
Hall throttles reach 2.5 to 3.0 V on a 3.3 V supply.
